abstract: Patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) mostly die from sudden cardiac death and recurrent heart failure. The mechanisms of cardiac remodeling are largely unclear. To dissect molecular and cellular mechanisms of cardiac remodeling in CKD in an unbiased fashion, we performed left ventricular single-nuclear RNA sequencing in two mouse models of CKD. Our data showed a hypertrophic response trajectory of cardiomyocytes with stress signaling and metabolic changes driven by soluble uremia-related factors. We mapped fibroblast to myofibroblast differentiation in this process and identified notable changes in the cardiac vasculature, suggesting inflammation and dysfunction. An integrated analysis of cardiac cellular responses to uremic toxins pointed toward endothelin-1 and methylglyoxal being involved in capillary dysfunction and TNFα driving cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in CKD, which was validated in vitro and in vivo. TNFα inhibition in vivo ameliorated the cardiac phenotype in CKD. Thus, interventional approaches directed against uremic toxins, such as TNFα, hold promise to ameliorate cardiac remodeling in CKD.

METHODS
Mice
Six- to 8-week-old male 129S2/SV mice (
n
= 7) were obtained from Envigo. Mice were group-housed and provided with ad lib access to water and standard chow, as well as environmental enrichment. A 12-hour light-dark cycle was maintained. During the study, mice were weighed weekly and had their condition recorded. ARRIVE guidelines were followed.
Animals were randomized to receive sham or STNx surgery using a random number generator website (random.org). In a single-step surgery, the right kidney was removed and the poles of the left kidney were cut, leaving one-third of it in place. For sham surgery, animals had bilateral flank incisions and both kidneys were isolated and manipulated. At 10 weeks, animals had a timed overnight urine collection and then were culled by an approved schedule 1 method, and terminal blood samples were obtained (
Fig. 1A
). For all animals, tibia length was recorded. Urine and serum were analyzed by in-house biochemical analysis service (surf.ed.ac.uk/facilities/specialist-assay-service/). A subset of STNx mice and of IRI mice was treated with etanercept (Enbrel, 5 mg/kg) every third day, starting from the surgery until the end of the experiment (fig. S8A).
Six 129S2/SvPasOrlRJ wild-type male mice underwent IRI plus uninephrectomy at the age of 11 and 12 weeks and were housed for 21 more weeks (
Fig. 1A
). Mice were anesthetized with ketamine/xylazine (120/16 mg/kg body weight), and after disinfection, flanks were incised, the right kidney was clamped for 26 min, and the contralateral kidney was fully removed. Mice received buprenorphine for three more days (0.1 mg/kg) to achieve analgesia. For genetic fate tracing of Gli1
+
cells, we bred bigenic Gli1CreER;tdTomato using Gli1tm3(re/ERT2)Alj/J (Jackson Laboratory stock no. 007913) and Rosa26tdTomato [i.e., B6-Cg-Gt(ROSA)26Sorttm(CAG-tdTomato)Hze/J, Jackson Laboratory stock no. 007909] mice. Six- to 7-week-old male mice (
n
= 7) received 3 × 2 mg tamoxifen in corn oil with 3% ethanol via intraperitoneal injection (every other day) to induce recombination and underwent the unilateral IRI plus contralateral nephrectomy surgery at 21 days after the last tamoxifen dose. Mice were killed 21 weeks after surgery, and the left ventricle was snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and transferred to −80°C. Serum urea was measured by clinical laboratory routine (Vitros 250, Ortho Clinical Diagnostics, Institut für Versuchstierkunde, Aachen). Heart weights were recorded (Sartorius 2007 MP, Germany) and normalized to tibia length, measured by a caliper (Forum, Germany).
Animal experiment protocols were approved by the Landesamt für Natur, Umwelt und Verbraucherschutz Nordrhein Westfalen LANUV-NRW, Germany and by the UK Home Office Regulations. All animal experiments were carried out in accordance with their guidelines.
Human hearts (
n
= 6 to 7) were collected as parts of the Cardiac Aging IN CKD CAIN cohort and by the National Disease Research Interchange (NDRI) and approved by the Partners Institutional Review Board (protocol no. 2017P001244/PHS).
Echocardiography
Echocardiography was performed on a Visualsonics Vevo 770 or 3100 in 2% isoflurane anesthesia. Thoracic fur was removed by depilatory cream, and mice were fixed on a heated table (37°C). A parasternal long-axis view of the heart was used to obtain electrocardiogram-gated kilohertz visualization over one cardiac cycle. Ejection fraction was measured by the Simpson’s method using four biplane views in B mode. Spectral Doppler was carried out in parasternal short-axis view and used to assess mitral valve and blood flow.
Millar
Hemodynamic parameters were measured by Millar catheter (Millar Instruments, USA). Mice were anesthetized with 10 μl/g body weight of ketamine (100 mg/kg) and xylazine (10 mg/kg), and 1 Fr Millar catheter (SPR 1000) was advanced across the right carotid artery through the aortic valve into the left ventricle. After hemodynamic stabilization, signals were continuously recorded and analyzed with iox (Emka Technologies, France). After a constant baseline signal, mice were injected with 5 μl/g body weight of dobutamine (1 mg/ml) to achieve maximal heart function.
Nuclei isolation
All steps were performed at 4°C. The same region from the apex of the snap-frozen left ventricle from each heart was cut and thawed in AW medium (Cellutron Life Technologies, USA). Left ventricular specimens from two mice hearts were pooled to one sample. Pieces were transferred to tris buffer [10 mM tris-HCl, 10 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl
2
, 0.1% NP-40, ribonuclease inhibitor (0.2 U/ml; Protector, Roche, Switzerland)] and 1× protease inhibitor (Roche cOmplete, Roche, Switzerland) in nuclease-free water (Invitrogen by Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). A tissue grinder was used to homogenize the tissues, and the lysate was incubated for 10 min on ice. The lysate was diluted with AW medium and further disrupted by pipetting up and down with a 2-ml glass pipette. The homogenate was filtered with a 70-μm cell strainer and centrifuged at 300
g
for 5 min. The pellet was washed twice with 1% bovine serum albumin (Ultra Pure, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) with protease inhibitor and filtered over a 40-μm cell strainer. The nuclei solution was subjected to single-nuclei sorting on a Sony SH800 cell sorter (Sony Biotechnologies, USA) over a 70-μm nozzle.
Single-nuclei sequencing
Next, nuclei were counted manually in a Neubauer chamber and loaded onto a 10× Chromium B chip and further processed according to the manufacturer’s´ instructions (Chromium Single-Cell Kit V3, 10x Genomics, USA). Briefly, gel beads in emulsion (GEM) were generated and barcoded (Chromium, 10x Genomics, USA). GEMs were cleaned, and complementary DNA (cDNA) was amplified on a thermal cycler (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). The cDNA was cleaned by SPRIselect beads, and a quality check was performed on a tape station. The cDNA library was generated after fragmentation, indexing, and double-sided size selection.
The library quality was determined using D1000 ScreenTape on a 2200 TapeStation system (Agilent Technologies, USA). Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq (Illumina Inc., USA) targeting a read depth as suggested by 10x Genomics 3′ single-cell RNA kits V2/3.
Cell culture
Human AC16 cardiomyocytes (Merck Millipore, USA) were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM)–F12 (D6434 Sigma-Aldrich, Germany) supplemented with 2 mM glutamine (TMS-002-C Millipore, USA), 12.5% fetal bovine serum (ES-009-B Millipore, USA), and 1% penicillin/streptomycin. For treatment, medium was supplemented either with 5 or 10% serum, pooled from healthy donors or pooled from dialysis patients, and incubated for 3 days at 37°C and 5% CO
2
. Cells were further treated with 100 nM Edn1 (Sigma-Aldrich, Germany), 500 nM ruxolitinib (Abcam, Germany) + 5% uremic serum or 50 μM etanercept + uremic serum, or vehicle for 3 days at 37°C and 5% CO
2
. For phosphoproteomics, AC16 cells and immortalized human cardiac PDGFRB cells (
59
) were treated with 5% healthy or 5% uremic serum for 90 min and 3 days. Afterward, PBS washed cells were lysed in 5% SDS, 5 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine, 10 mM chloroacetamide, and 100 mM tris (pH 8.5) at 95°C for 10 min.
HUVECs were isolated from primary tissue as previously described (
60
). Briefly, the umbilical cord vein was rinsed with 10% Hepes buffer (Life Technologies, Germany) using a butterfly syringe to remove the remaining blood. Afterward, the vein was filled with collagenase type I (330 U/ml; Worthington, USA), and the umbilical cord was incubated in 37°C prewarmed PBS (Gibco, Germany). To avoid leakage of collagenase, the umbilical cord was fixed with clamps. After 20 min, the vein was washed with 10 ml of 10% Hepes buffer in DMEM high glucose. Following a 7-min centrifugation step (200 g), the buffer was removed and the cell pellet was resuspended in 10 ml of EBM-2 Bullet Kit Medium (Lonza, Germany). Cells were seeded in a 75-cm
2
tissue culture flask coated with 2% gelatin (Sigma-Aldrich, Germany). After 24 hours, the first adherent island-like clusters with cobble-stone morphology were visible. HUVECs were cultured in a 20% O
2
, 5% CO
2
humidified atmosphere at 37°C. Endothelial cells were isolated from umbilical cords after cesarian sections and after informed consent, according to the standards of the local Ethics Committee (EK116/19).
For tube assay, HUVECs were cultured on Matrigel (Corning, Fisher Scientific, USA) overnight. Cells were treated with either uremic or healthy serum, as well as Edn1 protein (LS-
G26630
/108739, Biozol, Germany) or Edn1 neutralizing antibody (Ab 2786, Abcam, UK) to isotype control. Tubes were imaged on a BZ9001 Biorevo microscope (Keyence, Japan) and analyzed by the angiogenesis analyzer ImageJ plug-in (
61
).
The uremic serum was gathered from hemodialysis patients immediately before dialysis or healthy volunteers after informed consent. The study was approved by the ethical board of the RWTH Aachen University Hospital (Ethical Vote 347/15) and performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Cell lysis, protein extraction, and digestion
Cells were lysed with boiling SDS buffer [5% SDS, 5 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine, 10 mM chloroacetamide, and 100 mM tris (pH 8.5)]. Lysates were heated at 95°C for 10 min while shaking and further sonicated by microtip probe sonication (Vibra-Cell VCX130, Sonics, Newtown, CT) for 2 min with pulses of 1-s on and 1-s off at 70% amplitude. Protein concentration was estimated by bicinchoninic acid (Pierce).
Protein was digested using the protein aggregation capture protocol. One milligram of protein was resuspended with acetonitrile (ACN) to a final 70% concentration. MagReSyn Hydroxyl beads were added in a proportion of 1:2 (protein:beads). Protein aggregation was performed in two steps of 1-min mixing at 1000 rpm, followed by 10-min pause each. Beads were subsequently washed three times with 1 ml of 95% ACN and two times with 1 ml of 70% EtOH. Three hundred microliters of digestion buffer (50 mM ammonium bicarbonate) and proteases was added in the following proportions: trypsin 1:250 (enzyme:protein) and lysC 1:500 (enzyme:protein). Digestion was carried out overnight at 37°C with looping mixing. Protease activity was quenched by acidification with trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) to a final concentration of 1%.
Seven hundred fifty nanograms of digested peptides for single-shot proteome analysis was loaded on C18 Evotips (Evosep) for mass spectrometry (MS) analysis, and the remaining peptide mixture was concentrated on Sep-Pak (C18 Classic Cartridge, Waters, Milford, MA). Peptides were eluted with 150 μl of 40% ACN, followed by 150 μl of 60% ACN. The combined eluate was reduced by SpeedVac (Eppendorf, Germany), and the final peptide concentration was estimated by measuring absorbance at 280 nm on a NanoDrop 2000C spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific).
Phosphoproteomic enrichment
Fifty micrograms of peptides was dried by SpeedVac and resuspended with 200 μl of loading buffer (80% ACN, 5%TFA, and 1 M glycolic acid). Subsequent phospho-enrichment was performed in the King-fisher robot using 20 μl of MagReSyn Ti-IMAC HP beads (20 mg/ml). The unbound peptides were enriched a second time. Enriched phosphopeptides were acidified with 10% TFA until pH < 3, filtered to remove in-suspension particles (1 min, 500 g; MultiScreenHTS HV Filter Plate, 0.45 μm, clear, nonsterile), and loaded on C18 Evotips (Evosep) for MS analysis.
MS analysis
Samples were analyzed on the Evosep One system coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 480. Samples for proteome analysis were separated on an in-house packed 15-cm analytical column (150 μm inner diameter) and packed with 1.9-μm C18 beads, and column temperature was maintained at 60°C using an integrated column oven (PRSO-V1, Sonation GmbH). Samples for phosphoproteomics analysis were analyzed using EV-1112 column (PepSep; 15 cm × 75 μm, beads 1.9 μm) and EV-1087 emitter (fused silica, 20 μm). The column temperature was maintained at 40°C using a butterfly heater (PST-ES-BPH-20, Phoenix S&T) and interfaced online using an EASY-Spray source with the Orbitrap Exploris 480 MS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bremen, Germany) using Xcalibur. Preprogrammed gradients were used as follows: 30 samples per day for proteome and 20 samples per day for phosphoproteome (Whisper method).
The mass spectrometer was operated in a positive ion mode, with spray voltage at 2 kV for proteome and 1.8 kV for phosphoproteome. The heated capillary temperature was set at 275°C and the funnel radio frequency (RF) at 40. Peptide match was set to off, and isotope exclusion was on.
Data-independent acquisition (DIA) mode was used for both proteome and phosphoproteome. For proteome and phosphoproteome, full MS resolution was set to 120,000 at a mass/charge ratio (
m
/
z
) of 200, and full MS automatic gain control (AGC) target was set at 300%, with an injection time of 45 ms, and scan range was set to 350 to 1400
m
/
z
. AGC target value for fragment scan was set at 1000%. Normalized collision energy was set at 27%. For proteome, 49 windows of 13.7 Da were used with an overlap of 1 Da. The MS/MS acquisition was set to 15,000 resolution, and injection time was set to 22 ms. Normalized collision energy was set at 27%. For phosphoproteome, 26 windows of 25.9 Da were used with an overlap of 1 Da. The MS/MS acquisition was set to 30,000 resolution, and injection time was set to 54 ms.
MS raw data processing
DIA data were analyzed with Spectronaut v15.6.211220.50606 in directDIA mode with standard settings. The Human UniProt fasta file (downloaded in October 2020; 20,600 entries) was supplemented with a contaminant fasta file containing 246 entries.
Staining of tissue and cells
Cardiomyocytes were stained with tetramethylrhodamine (TMRM) (T668, Sigma-Aldrich, Germany) at 100 nM concentration and incubated for 30 min at 37°C. Images were taken on a Nikon A1 laser confocal microscope (Nikon, Tokio, Japan).
To analyze the size of cardiomyocytes and the capillary density, tissue sections were rehydrated and heat-induced antigen retrieval was performed in citrate buffer. Slides were incubated with fluorescein-coupled WGA (1:100; FL-1021, Vector Laboratories) and CD31 (1:50; AF3628, R&D Systems) and further counterstained with DAPI. Slides were digitalized using Aperio Versa200 whole-slide scanner (Leica Biosystems, Germany). For each mouse, three areas from the inner part of the left ventricle were analyzed using ImageJ (National Institutes of Health). About 600 to 1100 cross-cut cardiomyocytes were measured to determine the area and minFeret. Capillary density was measured as length of capillaries per unit volume of myocardial tissue (
3
). All analyses were performed in a blinded manner. Collagens were visualized in blue by Masson-Goldner trichrome staining (Sigma-Aldrich, Germany).
In situ hybridizations were performed with the RNAscope multiplex fluorescent reagent kit V2 assay (ACD, Biotechne, USA) on heart cryosections, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Probes were designed against
Pecam1
and
Edn1
. Sections were counterstained with DAPI, embedded in Immumount, and imaged on a Nikon A1 laser confocal microscope (Nikon, Tokio, Japan).
Single-cell RNA analysis
We preprocessed scRNA-seq sequencing data for each library with cellranger pipeline (v3.1.0) using the default parameters. Next, we used Seurat [v3.2.0; (
62
)] to perform the integration and clustering. We first created a Seurat object from the count matrix. Next, we filtered cells by only retaining cells with nFeatureRNAfloor of >400 and nCountRNAceilling of <40,000. We used the function FindIntegrationAchors and IntegrateData to integrate samples followed by calling the function FindNeighbors and FindClusters (resolution = 0.5) to find communities on principal components analysis (PCA) embedding space (pcs = 30).
Differentially expressed genes enrichment analysis
We retrieved highly expressed differential marker genes using FindAllMarkers and annotated clusters with curated markers. Next, we applied clusterProfiler [v3.18.0; (
63
)] to do GO, KEGG analysis, and inferred pathway activity using PROGENY [v1.11.3; (
64
)]. To compare the following phenotypes hypertrophy and angiogenesis, we considered the following gene sets from Harmonizome (
65
), respectively: (i) [Cardiomyocytes, (
https://maayanlab.cloud/Harmonizome/gene_set/Hypertrophy/CTD+Gene-Disease+Associations
, standardizedValue>2)] and (ii) (Capillary changes,
https://maayanlab.cloud/Harmonizome/gene_set/angiogenesis/GeneRIF+Biological+Term+Annotations
). The ECM gene set used in this study was obtained from Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA). Specifically, the ECM gene set corresponds to the NABA_CORE_MATRISOME item included in MSigDB. To plot ridges of these gene sets, we calculated the gene module score(
x
axis) by summing the gene expressions and obtaining the log-normalized value of the score.
Trajectory inference
To do trajectory analysis for a specific cell type population, we first selected a subpopulation of this cell type. Next, we embedded the PCA to a diffusion map using destiny [v3.4.0; (
64
,
66
)], followed by clustering on the embedding space. We performed the similar strategy of ArchR [v1.0.1; (
67
)] to do the trajectory analysis. We first defined a backbone by selecting cluster IDs. Next, we calculated mean coordinates for each cluster and Euclidean distance of each cell from cluster i to mean coordinate of cluster i + 1. Next, we fitted a trajectory using smooth spline function and scaled the pseudotime to 100. To construct genes along the trajectory matrix, we first split cells to 100 groups by their pseudotime ranges. We next summed up each group of cells to get a matrix, followed by log-normalizing on the matrix. The GO term matrix was constructed on the basis of the genes along the trajectory matrix. We first split the pseudotime into five groups, and we decided the group of each gene by its highest mean expression of the group. With the five gene sets, we then ran GO enrichment to get the GO terms along the trajectory.
LR-based cell-cell cross-talk
The cellular cross-talk analysis was done by CellPhoneDB (CPDB, v2.0.5) for each phenotype separately. Initially, scRNA-seq matrices were log-normalized and scaled using Seurat functions. Next, we used CPDB to infer putative LR pairs using the “statistical_analysis” mode. We expanded the LR data sources to consider further sources besides the one provided by CPDB (
68
) [TalkLR (
68
,
69
), scTensor (
69
,
70
), SCA (
71
), and iTALK (
72
)]. Interactions with at least two consensus data sources were kept in the final LR database. Last, the significant interactions identified by CPDB were analyzed regarding network properties and visualized by CrossTalkeR [v1.0.0,
https://github.com/CostaLab/CrossTalkeR
; (
72
,
73
)].
UT gene set analysis
The analysis of UTs was done considering the UT database (
74
). For each toxin presented in the UT database, we retrieved the gene set related to it from Harmonizome repository (
65
), which was obtained by the GeneRIF (
65
,
75
). We then performed GSEA comparing distinct models to find cell types with high levels of expression of genes associated to UTs.
RNA-seq analysis
We aligned RNA-seq fastq files to GRCh38 genome and performed transcript quantification using the nf-core/rnaseq (v3.0) nextflow pipeline (
76
) (v21.04.0). Next, we performed gene expression differentiation with DESeq2. The same hypertrophy gene set aforementioned was used to compare the Human AC16 model. PROGENY [v1.11.3; (
64
,
76
)] was also applied to infer pathway activity.
snRNA-seq heart failure comparison
We analyzed the snRNA-seq data from human heart failure (
14
) to compare it with the signaling pathway analysis conducted in our mouse model. First, we used the mouse data as a reference to integrate the human data and transferred labels using Symphony (
77
). Next, we performed PROGENY analysis to compare DCM with the donor condition for each transferred cell type. We checked the disease pathway regulation direction(r effect size) between DCM model and our model, set ✓ when the regulation direction agree with each other, and set ✗ when disagree (see fig. S4, A and B). We also examined the angiotensin II fibrosis model (
15
). Following a similar approach, we used our snRNA-seq mouse data as a reference to integrate and transfer labels to the angiotensin II fibrosis model data. Similar disease pathway regulation direction comparison between angiotensin II fibrosis model and our model was also performed to check the consistency between two models in each cell type (see fig. S4, C and D).
Statistics
Further parameters were analyzed by D’Agoustino Pearson normality test and visual classification to check for a Gaussian distribution. Student’s
t
test with independent variance was applied to check for differences between two groups for parametric data. Three groups were compared by ordinary one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with multiple comparisons as a follow-up test. The significance level was set to
P
< 0.05. The software GraphPad Prism 9 and IBM statistics SPSS 26 were used. Student’s
t
test was also applied to compare PROGENY pathway differences and gene set differences. Fisher’s exact test was performed to test cell population differences between two conditions.

INTRODUCTION
The global prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) has reached over 10% in the developed world and is still increasing at a rate of up to 8% annually (
1
). CKD is an increasingly urgent public health concern, and patients with CKD suffer from tremendously increased cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, with recurrent heart failure and sudden cardiac death being the leading causes of death in end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) (
2
). In ESKD, adverse cardiac remodeling occurs, which describes morphological changes in the left ventricle with cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, cardiac fibrosis, and capillary dysfunction and loss of capillaries (
3
). While the proinflammatory uremic milieu and vascular stiffening with increased afterload as well as hypertension are known to be involved, we lack a complete and integrative understanding of cellular and molecular mechanisms of this remodeling process, which results in systolic and diastolic left ventricular dysfunction with the development of heart failure and sudden cardiac death (
2
). The process is in part reversible after kidney transplantation, suggesting that the identification of uremia-associated factors might potentially result in novel therapeutic approaches.
To untangle the complex cellular and molecular mechanisms in cardiac remodeling in CKD in an unbiased fashion, we here performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) from the left ventricle of mice subjected to two different models of CKD with cardiac remodeling. We identified all major cell types of the mammalian heart and identified distinct transcriptional changes that drive pathophysiology including cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, cardiac fibrosis, and capillary dysfunction. We performed inducible genetic fate tracing of cardiac fibroblasts combined with single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to increase resolution on transcriptional changes in fibroblast to myofibroblast differentiation driving cardiac fibrosis in uremic cardiomyopathy. In particular, we addressed tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα) inhibition on cardiomyocytes in vitro and in vivo. Our data provide evidence for roles of three uremic toxins (UTs) in cardiac remodeling in CKD, namely, endothelin-1 (Edn1), methylglyoxal (MGO), and TNFα.
RESULTS
Modeling uremic cardiomyopathy in mice
To induce cardiac remodeling in CKD, we used two distinct mouse models: (i) subtotal nephrectomy (STNx) and (ii) ischemia reperfusion injury (IRI) with contralateral nephrectomy (
Fig. 1A

Fig. 1, B and C
). We noticed an increased heart weight (corrected for tibia length) in both models as compared to sham (
Fig. 1B
). Kidney functional parameters and also the left ventricular ejection fraction at the time point of sacrifice were significantly reduced in both models (
Fig. 1, B and C
). Trends were found for prolongation in ejection time and increase in the peak velocity flow of the early diastole to velocity flow of the late diastole (E/A) in IRI mice, as well as reduction of stroke volume in both models (table S1A). Corresponding genes involved in cardiomyocyte contraction seem to be more altered after IRI, especially a decrease in
Myh6
and
Mybp3
, which also relate to dilative cardiomyopathies (fig. S1) (

Signaling pathway analysis using pathway-responsive genes for activity interference (PROGENY) revealed up-regulation of various profibrotic and proinflammatory pathways [e.g., Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT), nuclear factor κB (NFκB), TNFα, and hypoxia] across various cell types (including cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, macrophages, and VSMCs) in both models of cardiac remodeling in CKD compared to sham (
Fig. 1F
). This finding was more pronounced in the STNx model as compared to the IRI model (
Fig. 1F
). Activation of TNFα and NFκB indicated a proinflammatory response (
5
,
6

7
). We detected down-regulation of TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL), phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K), and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling in several cell types including pericytes, fibroblasts, and cardiomyocytes in both models compared to sham (
Fig. 1F
).
Because not all mRNA is translated into protein and signaling pathways are often regulated by reversible protein phosphorylation, we performed phosphoproteomic analysis of human, left ventricular platelet-derived growth factor β (PDGFRB) cells and of human, ventricular AC16 cardiomyocytes incubated with pooled uremic and pooled control serum. This allows us to compare with observations found in mice and to verify uremic milieu–driven alterations in pathway activities and abundance of proteins. We detected pronounced changes by uremic serum indicating matrix remodeling in PDGFRB cells by up-regulation of extracellular matrix protein 1 (Ecm1) and fibulin 1 (Fbln1) protein, similar to our observation in the STNx mice at the mRNA level (fig. S3, A and B). The proangiogenic mediator anthrax toxin receptor (Antxr), which can bind to the extracellular matrix (ECM) (
8
), was up-regulated at the protein level in PDGFRB cells in vitro and RNA level in fibroblasts and pericytes in vivo (fig. S3, B and D). Increased mitogen-activated protein kinase 6 (MAPK6) activity was identified by increased phosphorylation at serine-189 in human PDGFRB cells exposed to uremic serum, while we observed increased MAPK6 mRNA expression in STNx mice compared to controls (fig. S3, B and D). Regulated genes downstream of MAPK6, including
Pcna
,
Ccnd1
, and
Mmp2
(
9
), were mainly up-regulated in fibroblasts and pericytes in hearts from STNx mice (fig. S3C). Stress-activated MAPK pathways play a role in cardiac hypertrophy and can be activated by reactive oxygen species (ROS) or Edn1 (
10
). We further observed increased phosphorylation of cut-like homeobox 1 (Cux1) in PDGFRB cells exposed to uremic serum, which can be induced by transforming growth factor β (Tgfb) (
11
). These data point toward ongoing inhibitory actions by Cux1 on TRAIL, profibrotic, and antiapoptotic effects (
12
).
Cux1
was also up-regulated at the mRNA level in STNx mice especially in pericytes and fibroblasts, as well as in macrophages and monocytes (fig. S3, B and E). In AC16 cardiomyocytes, the EGF responder Rbm3 was phosphorylated after stimulation with uremic serum, and we observed increased mRNA expression of RNA binding motif protein 3 (
Rbm3
) in STNx mice (fig. S3, B and F).
Rbm3
was described earlier to be involved in skeletal muscle hypertrophy (
13
).
To compare the signature of our uremic models to other cardiomyopathies, we reanalyzed single nuclei sequencing data from human heart failure (
14
), as well as cardiac single-cell sequencing data of a murine angiotensin II infusion model (
15
). In the human heart failure data, most cell types showed increased JAK-STAT, hypoxia, estrogen, and androgen pathways compared to healthy controls (fig. S4, A and B). Comparing these human data to our STNx model data by their effect sizes revealed similar regulations in TRAIL, Wnt, JAK-STAT, hypoxia, and androgen pathways in most cell types. In fibroblasts, pronounced and a similar down-regulation of TRAIL but up-regulations of MAPK and JAK-STAT were identified (fig. S4A). Comparing the human dilative cardiomyopathy to our uremic IRI mouse model revealed similarities in TRAIL, hypoxia, and androgen pathway regulations in most cell types. In particular, in cardiomyocytes, we identified similar up-regulation of TNFα and p53 pathways (fig. S4B). Compared to both of our models, the biggest differences were seen in Tgfb and EGFR activities in the major cell types, as well as NFκB and EGFR in fibroblasts and PI3K in pericytes (fig. S4, A and B).
The cardiac scRNA-seq data of the murine angiotensin II model (
15
) showed increased Tgfb signaling activity across major cell types (fig. S4, C and D). Comparing the angiotensin II data to our uremic cardiomyopathy models indicated a similar signaling of Tgfb in most cell types and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling in endothelial cells (fig. S4, C and D). TNFα, NFκB, JAK-STAT, and MAPK were among the pathways that were differentially regulated in the major cell types between our uremic cardiomyopathy models and the angiotensin II infusion model.
In contrast to two other cardiomyopathies, high NFκB pathway activity was found in fibroblasts, which gave uremic cardiomyopathy a distinctive characteristic (figs. S1F and S4, A to D). When comparing the cell type distribution in our CKD models to sham controls, we noticed the strongest changes in abundance of mesothelial cells that significantly increased in both models (fig. S5A). The mesothelium can contribute to inflammation and fibrosis by secreting proinflammatory chemokines or growth factors, but it is also essential for cardiac injury repair (
16
). A second major cell type that showed significant alterations in both CKD models comprised endothelial cells with an increased abundance of certain endothelial subpopulations in both models (fig. S5A).
To gain insight into potential cellular cross-talk partners during cardiac remodeling in CKD, we next performed receptor-ligand interaction analyses. In homeostasis, we noticed strong autocrine signaling of mesothelial cells in the sham condition, which was attenuated in both disease models (
Fig. 1G
). In the STNx model, we saw strongly increased cellular signaling between various cell types including fibroblasts, monocytes, pericytes, and VSMCs as compared to sham (
Fig. 1G
), which was reflected in the cluster importance scoring of these cells in cell-cell communication analysis (fig. S5B). In the IRI model, this difference was alleviated with only slightly increased cross-talk between monocytes, cardiomyocytes, and fibroblasts (
Fig. 1G
). Ranking the affected pathways by their activity (Pagerank) revealed greater overlap in our two models. In both models, highly active pathways included focal adhesion, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), ECM receptor interactions, and (receptor for) advanced glycation end products (AGE-RAGE) in diabetic complications (fig. S6, A to F). This confirms active structural processes such as profibrotic processes and hypertrophic responses, as well as further pathological processes in both mouse models carved out by their highly active receptors and ligands.

Fig. 2, A and B
). We noticed a significantly increased expression of a hypertrophy-related gene set in all cardiomyocyte clusters in both models (
Fig. 2C
).

Diffusion mapping is a dimensionality reduction method that assumes that cells relate to each other by a differentiation-like diffusion process (
17
). To gain insight into the hypertrophic response of cardiomyocytes, we clustered all cardiomyocyte subtypes and performed diffusion map embedding and pseudotime trajectory analysis (
Fig. 2, D to G
). These data suggested a differentiation trajectory toward cardiomyocytes 2 (
Fig. 2, E and F
), which showed the highest enrichment of the hypertrophy gene set (
Fig. 2G
). We next sorted genes and gene ontology (GO) terms along the differentiation trajectory pseudotime (
Fig. 2, H and I
). This analysis indicated cardiomyocyte-specific genes such as
Sorbs2
,
Camk2d
, and
Fam13a
being enriched at the beginning of the trajectory, while genes associated with mechanical stress such as
Nppa
,
Adam15
, and
Mcf2lb
(
18
), and genes pointing toward an altered metabolism such as
Hadha
(
19
) were enriched toward the end of the trajectory (
Fig. 2H
). Notably, the metalloprotease Adam15 has been reported to be involved in cardiac dilation by reducing cell matrix interactions via integrin shedding (
20
).
Early enriched GO terms along the hypertrophy trajectory included structural components, such as actinin binding, microtubule end, and calcineurin/calcium signaling, while terms such as cellular response to Tgfb, ECM organization, mitochondrial protein complex, and ribosomes were enriched toward the end of the trajectory, in line with increased cellular stress and compensation mechanisms (
Fig. 2I
).
As cardiomyocytes 2 was the population that showed the strongest enrichment of hypertrophy-associated genes and showed enrichment toward the presumed hypertrophic differentiation trajectory, we next compared the top differentially expressed genes and GO terms within this cluster between the two CKD models and sham.
Nppb
,
Vegfa
, and
Sorbs2
were among the most up-regulated genes in STNx compared to sham, while
Nppa
and
Myl3
were highly up-regulated in IRI compared to sham (fig. S7A). The top up-regulated GO terms of cardiomyocytes 2 include acetylcholine signaling, hypertrophic response in STNx, as well as up-regulations of the lipids and fatty acid metabolism and muscle contraction in IRI (fig. S7, B and C).
To gain insight into potential cellular cross-talk events that might be involved in this hypertrophic cardiomyocyte remodeling process, we next performed receptor-ligand analysis only considering intercellular signaling from or to cardiomyocytes and with only including cardiomyocyte ligand or receptors within the hypertrophic gene set. This analysis pointed toward an increased communication of cardiomyocytes with fibroblasts, monocytes, and pericytes in both models, compared to sham (fig. S7H). Looking deeper at the communication signals toward cardiomyocytes, we observed a close connection of the hypertrophic response to fibrosis with
Col3a1
and
Col4a1
expressed by fibroblasts and signaling to cardiomyocytes via integrin beta receptor 1 (Itgb1) and kinase insert domain receptor (Kdr) in STNx. Furthermore, we noticed thrombospondin 1 (
Thbs1
) signaling from pericytes toward several cardiomyocyte populations (fig. S7D). In the IRI model, cardiomyocytes seem to stimulate themselves with lipoprotein lipase (
Lpl
), which has been reported to increase lipid uptake in cardiomyopathy (fig. S7E) (
21
). To further clarify the cell-cell interactions of cardiomyocytes 2 with all other cell types, we performed a downstream analysis including all genes (fig. S7, F and G). Up-regulation of PI3K-Akt signaling, focal adhesion, and ECM receptor interactions in cardiomyocytes 2 with most other cell types after STNx points toward ECM remodeling (fig. S7F). Highly regulated pathways after IRI included calcium signaling, ras-associated protein 1 (Rap1) signaling, and EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor regulations (fig. S7G). Overall, several pathways involved in the communication with cardiomyocytes 2 are down-regulated after IRI (fig. S7G).
To verify the murine data in a human system and to understand which of these responses can be attributed to uremia, we stimulated human AC16 cardiomyocytes with uremic serum. This resulted in a significant increase in cardiomyocyte size, compared to healthy serum (
Fig. 2K
), suggesting that soluble uremic factors were involved in the hypertrophic response of cardiomyocytes in CKD. We next performed bulk RNA sequencing from the cardiomyocytes subjected to healthy or uremic serum. These data indicated enrichment of the hypertrophy gene set after treatment with 5% uremic serum, as expected (
Fig. 2L
). Up-regulated pathways in the cardiomyocytes exposed to uremic serum were JAK-STAT, NFκB, p53, and TNFα (
Fig. 2M
). The JAK-STAT pathway responds to stress signals and mediates growth signals to the hypertrophic heart (
22
). TNFα receptors can be stimulated by various stimuli that could be present in uremic serum, and the main ligand TNFα is indeed considered a UT (
www.uremic-toxins.org
). TNFα has been shown to induce cardiac hypertrophy; this can be partially driven by TNFα-induced activation of NFκB (
23
). Our in vitro perturbation data of human cells confirmed the in vivo data from mouse cardiomyocytes, where JAK-STAT, NFκB, p53, and TNFɑ pathways were significantly up-regulated (
Fig. 1L
). We next sought to validate the roles of JAK-STAT and TNFα in uremic serum–induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in vitro. Blocking the JAK-STAT pathway by ruxolitinib did result in a significant decrease of uremic serum–induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy (
Fig. 2M
). However, the TNFα inhibitor etanercept was capable to fully block hypertrophy, induced by uremic serum (
Fig. 2M
), validating the role of TNFα as a soluble uremia-induced factor on cardiac hypertrophy.
To further validate the role of TNFα, we performed a mouse experiment with TNFα inhibition using etanercept in both models over time (fig. S8A). Inhibition of TNFα ameliorated the phenotype at 11 weeks after injury in the IRI model as indicated by a significantly better ejection fraction as compared to the control group (fig. S8B). STNx mice treated with etanercept had significantly lower heart weights (fig. S8C) and had a trend toward improved ejection fraction (fig. S8B). In the IRI model, which was a long-term model over 21 weeks, we did not detect significant differences at the late time point comparing etanercept treatment to the control group (table S1B).

To gain more insight into this population, we next looked at differentially expressed genes as well as GO terms and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways in fibroblasts 2 comparing sham to the two CKD models (fig. Fabp3
was among the top differentially expressed genes in fibroblasts 2 comparing IRI to sham (fig. S9B). Both

and
Fabp3
have been reported as regulators of myofibroblast differentiation in kidney or liver (

To better understand the cardiac fibroblast activation and differentiation process in CKD, we performed diffusion map embedding and pseudotime trajectory analyses of the fibroblast clusters (
Fig. 3D
). These analyses suggested a trajectory of differentiation that showed increased expression of
Col1a1
and
Postn
along fibroblast to myofibroblast differentiation. We also observed increased

expression along this trajectory (
Fig. 3B
), which we recently identified as an important ECM regulator in human kidney myofibroblasts (
28
,
29

Slit3
and
Gli3
enriched in early differentiation followed by
Pdgfra
,
Smad2
,
Jun
, and
Col1a1
expression (
Fig. 3E
), i.e., genes known to play a role in fibrosis. We have reported an important role of Hedgehog Gli and Fos-Jun in fibrosis (
24
,
30

Smad2
is an important downstream member of Tgfb signaling, a well-known master regulator of fibrosis, and several lines of evidence suggest an important role of Pdgfr signaling in the proliferation of mesenchymal cells in fibrosis (
31

32

Fig. 3D

The receptor-ligand signaling analysis focused on fibroblasts as senders or receivers pointed toward increased signaling with cardiomyocytes, macrophages, monocytes, pericytes, and VSMCs in the STNx model. In the IRI model, this signaling increase was attenuated with mild increases of signals from cardiomyocytes, pericytes, and macrophages as compared to sham (
Fig. 3G

Fbn

CCL21 is a chemokine that has been reported to predict cardiovascular mortality after myocardial infarction (

34

35

+

To verify these data and increase the resolution on cardiac fibrosis driving cells, we next moved to genetic fate tracing experiments using bigenic Gli1CreER;tdTomato mice. These mice recombine in cardiac fibrosis driving cells, as previously demonstrated in fate tracing and ablation experiments (

33

Fig. 4A
). Twenty weeks after the surgery, mice were killed and organs were harvested. We noticed only minor interstitial and perivascular fibrotic lesions in the myocardium without strong enrichment of tdTomato
+
fate-traced cells (
Fig. 4B
). Serum urea was slightly but significantly increased at the time point of sacrifice, indicating the development of CKD (
Fig. 4C
). The echocardiographic analysis showed a significant decrease in the stroke volume in the CKD group compared to sham (fig. S10A). In addition, the maximum left ventricular pressure (dp/dtmax) under dobutamine stimulation was significantly reduced in the CKD group compared to sham (
Fig. 4D
), indicating early left ventricular functional impairment. However, the other functional parameters remained unchanged (table S2 and fig. S10A). Following sacrifice, the left ventricle was digested and tdTomato
+
cells were sorted for subsequent scRNA-seq (
Fig. 4E
). We included
n
= 5318 high-quality cells in the analysis from eight mice (
n
= 2 libraries per model with two pooled mice per library). Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embedding visualized one large fibroblast cluster consisting of six fibroblast subpopulations, one myofibroblast cluster, and one pericyte cluster (
Fig. 4F
). The cell type distribution analysis indicated a threefold expansion of myofibroblasts in the CKD group, while the abundance of other cell types had moderate changes (
Fig. 4G
). We next looked at the overall ECM expression. While we did not detect a significant increase of ECM expression within individual cell clusters (fig. S10B), we noticed the overall highest ECM expression in myofibroblasts (
Fig. 4H

) was higher in STNx compared to sham (fig. S14B). Cardiac
Edn1
expression was mostly unchanged (fig. S14C). Downstream genes of
Ednra
, in particular
Mmp14
,
Vcam
, and
Egr1
(
42
), point toward active
Ednra
signaling especially in fibroblasts (fig. S14, D to F). Downstream genes of
Ednrb
, selectively
Cxcl1
,
Lepr
, and
Nppb
(
42
), point toward active
Ednrb
signaling in fibroblasts and cardiomyocytes, and monocytes (fig. S14, G to I). To validate the role of Edn1 on endothelial cells, we used a tube formation angiogenesis assay. First, we analyzed the effects of human uremic serum in comparison to healthy serum on tube formation of human umbilical cord endothelial cells (HUVECs). Treatment with 20% uremic serum significantly increased the length of isolated endothelial cell branches (
Fig. 6B
) and the number of isolated segments, while all other parameters remained unchanged (table S3A). This indicates that the overall endothelial cell tube network does not decrease but shows fewer connections in the uremic condition pointing toward potential dysfunction. To test the potential role of Edn1 in this system, we next added either recombinant Edn1 or a neutralizing Edn1 antibody. Recombinant Edn1 did not show an effect on tube formation, while the neutralizing antibody significantly increased the tube formation of HUVECs, as indicated by the total meshes area (
Fig. 6C
) and increased branching interval (table S3B). These data suggest that there might be Edn1 activity in the cell culture medium, presumably in the serum, and that this Edn1 might affect tube formation directly. We found up-regulations of endothelin conversion enzyme 1 in endothelial cells of both models (
Fig. 6D
). This enzyme is essential for the activation of Edn1. To validate the role of Edn1 on cardiomyocytes, we incubated AC16 cardiomyocytes for 3 days with recombinant human Edn1. Edn1 induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy (
Fig. 6E

Edn1
was mainly derived from nonendothelial cells (fig. S11, F to J).
Edn1
-positive cells of all cells [4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) positive] were significantly up-regulated in hearts from heart failure + CKD compared to healthy control hearts (fig. S11G). Whereas
Edn1
-positive cells of
Pecam1
-positive cells only tended to be higher in hearts from patients with heart failure and CKD (fig. S11H),
Edn1
-positive and
Pecam1
-negative cells were significantly up-regulated in hearts from heart failure + CKD compared to healthy controls, as well as compared to heart failure (fig. S11I). The overall cell count (DAPI-positive cells) remained stable, but
Pecam1

In the IRI model, the computational analysis of UTs revealed a significant impact of MGO on endothelial cells (fig. S13A). MGO was shown earlier to trigger endothelial dysfunction in human vascular disease (
43

MGO treatment resulted in a dose-dependent reduction of total HUVEC mesh area as well as in a significant reduction of the total length of the tubes (fig. S13D).
Overall, these data suggest that receptors for various UTs are expressed in cardiac cells and that CKD induces gene expression alterations of these receptors. Our data provide novel evidence for roles of three UTs in cardiac remodeling in CKD: Edn1, MGO, and TNFα.
DISCUSSION
Recurrent heart failure and sudden cardiac death are the major causes of mortality in patients with end-stage renal disease (
44
). Beyond traditional risk factors of cardiovascular disease, various nontraditional risk factors, such as UTs, are thought to drive cardiac remodeling in CKD (
45
). The exact cellular and molecular mechanisms of cardiac remodeling in CKD are, however, unclear to date. We present the first unbiased map of cardiac remodeling in CKD using two distinct mouse models of CKD. These data included all major cardiac cells, allowing precise comparison of transcriptional signatures in response to CKD. Our data enabled us to model the hypertrophic response of cardiomyocytes in CKD and point toward interesting roles of mechanical stress, metabolism, and UTs.
A hallmark of cardiac remodeling in CKD is fibrosis. We demonstrated here that fibroblasts are the major cellular source of cardiac fibrosis in CKD and present a differentiation trajectory of fibroblasts to myofibroblasts with up-regulation of several known fibrosis regulatory genes including
Tgfb
,
Jun
,
Pdgfra
, collagens, and periostin in line with mechanisms of fibrosis in other organs such as the kidney (
31
). We validated the role of fibroblast to myofibroblast differentiation using combined genetic fate tracing and scRNA-seq in Gli1CreER;tdTomato mice. We observed a potential role of TRAIL signaling in this process. TRAIL signaling has been reported to regulate fibrosis in other organs such as the lung and the liver (
46
,
47
). The data allowed us to precisely model fibroblast to myofibroblast differentiation in CKD.
Capillary dysfunction and loss have been reported as another potentially important mechanism in uremic cardiomyopathy (
3
). We observed capillary changes in both models of CKD. Following IRI, we noticed a reduced expression of an angiogenic gene set, which could be interpreted as a failed response because in the hypertrophic remodeling process angiogenesis would be required. In the STNx model, we observed an inflammatory, proangiogenic transcriptomic response suggesting capillary dysfunction. VEGF signaling was up-regulated in several endothelial clusters in both models, while we also observed increased endothelial TNFα, TRAIL, Tgfb, and NFκB pathway activity. Several studies have suggested that lower TRAIL concentration predicts poor prognosis in patients with cardiovascular disease (
48
). We had opposite effects on TRAIL in the different models. Proteomics and transcriptomics revealed an increase of
Cux1
, a downstream target of
Tgfb
, which inhibits TRAIL (
12
). In STNx, we identified an up-regulation of TNFα activity, which, in contrast, can stimulate TRAIL. PI3K signaling is involved in various processes including angiogenesis and calcium handling in response to catecholamines and plays an important role in heart failure (
49
), while EGFR signaling has also been reported to be involved in cardiac remodeling (
50
).
While macrophages have been reported as key cellular players in myocardial homeostasis and disease (
51
), we did not find significant numerical changes of macrophage populations between disease and control tissue except for a decrease of macrophages 2 in IRI (fig. S5A). Macrophages 1 are likely reparatory macrophages (
Il10ra
and
Pdgfc
;
Fig. 1F
). In IRI, macrophages 1 reduce the secretion of
Pdgfc
(
Fig. 5J
) (
52
). Pdgfc exhibits multiple effects, including proangiogenic and profibrotic actions (
53
). Macrophages 2 are likely inflammatory macrophages (
Csf1r
and
Irf
). In STNx, macrophages 2 secrete more
Lamc1
(fig. S12D), which is essential for vascular development and organization (
54
).
Cellular cross-talk events are considered key in tissue homeostasis and disease. Modeling of receptor-ligand interactions suggested heavily down-regulated signaling pathways in cardiac remodeling in CKD. This indicates a loss of homeostasis-related cell-cell communication in CKD. However, there are certain limitations of the model because it does solely look at mRNA expression of receptors and ligands, which does not necessarily translate into increased or decreased signaling. Therefore, we have, for some of the pathways, also looked at downstream target genes or performed comparison to in vitro (phospho-) proteomics. The receptor-ligand analysis suggested that cardiac mesothelial cells lose their self-communication, probably contributing to decreased cellular homeostasis and self-repair. The mesothelium has been reported to be critical in regulating fibrosis and inflammation (
16
). Notably, uremic pericarditis is an important complication of kidney failure and occurs as a result of inflammation likely due to UTs (
55
). The pericardial fluid, which is secreted by the mesothelium changes during pericarditis and potentially increased toxins and inflammatory signals in this fluid, might disrupt mesothelial cell function driving inflammation and dysfunction of the pericardium.
We observed increased cellular cross-talk of cardiomyocytes with fibroblasts, monocytes, and pericytes. The data suggested signaling activity that likely drives cardiac remodeling, hypertrophy, and fibrosis. One single gene that we found up-regulated not only in hypertrophic cardiomyocytes but also in fibroblasts 2 and endothelial cells was
Nppa
. This gene encodes for a peptide regulating salt and water balance and has been reported as an important player in cardiac hypertrophy and vascular remodeling (
56
). Its up-regulation is a sign of cardiac stress (
57
). As major players in the uremic hypertrophic response, we identified Edn1 and TNFα. Inhibition of the latter by etanercept fully normalized uremia-induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in vitro. In vivo, our data suggested a clear effect of TNFα inhibition with reduced heart weight at sacrifice in the STNx model and improved ejection fraction in the IRI model at the 11-week time point. However, at the late time point, in the IRI model, we did not observe a significant effect. These data support a role of TNFα and inflammation in cardiac remodeling in CKD; however, at the same time, there are various other mechanisms driving cardiac pathophysiology in CKD, and thus, a single interventional approach is unlikely the best way to approach this complex disease. Nevertheless, our work points toward an increased inflammatory state in CKD with the known UT TNFα being critically involved.
In this study, we have mapped numerous complex alterations in the signaling of two different models of uremic cardiomyopathy. The strength is the non–hypothesis-driven approach to identify underlying mechanisms and potential contributing signaling pathways and UTs. A limitation of this study lies in the differences of the applied mouse models, which do not always lead to a similar outcome, especially concerning angiogenic gene sets in the endothelium. However, proangiogenic and antiangiogenic responses are implicated in different types of cardiac diseases. Besides, a bias in the cell population distribution or in the hypertrophic response of cardiomyocytes cannot be fully excluded. One reason for this potential bias could be due to the different quality of the samples, possibly originating from the nuclei isolation. We cannot exclude an overestimation of cardiomyocyte cell number in our data because some cardiomyocytes are multinucleated (
58
).
In summary, our data provide novel insights into cellular and molecular mechanisms driving cardiac remodeling after injury to the kidney and point toward important roles of the UTs MGO, Edn1, and TNFα. Interventional strategies directed against specific UTs and associated cytokines hold promise to ameliorate the cardiac phenotype in advanced CKD.
METHODS
Mice
Six- to 8-week-old male 129S2/SV mice (
n
= 7) were obtained from Envigo. Mice were group-housed and provided with ad lib access to water and standard chow, as well as environmental enrichment. A 12-hour light-dark cycle was maintained. During the study, mice were weighed weekly and had their condition recorded. ARRIVE guidelines were followed.
Animals were randomized to receive sham or STNx surgery using a random number generator website (random.org). In a single-step surgery, the right kidney was removed and the poles of the left kidney were cut, leaving one-third of it in place. For sham surgery, animals had bilateral flank incisions and both kidneys were isolated and manipulated. At 10 weeks, animals had a timed overnight urine collection and then were culled by an approved schedule 1 method, and terminal blood samples were obtained (
Fig. 1A
). For all animals, tibia length was recorded. Urine and serum were analyzed by in-house biochemical analysis service (surf.ed.ac.uk/facilities/specialist-assay-service/). A subset of STNx mice and of IRI mice was treated with etanercept (Enbrel, 5 mg/kg) every third day, starting from the surgery until the end of the experiment (fig. S8A).
Six 129S2/SvPasOrlRJ wild-type male mice underwent IRI plus uninephrectomy at the age of 11 and 12 weeks and were housed for 21 more weeks (
Fig. 1A
). Mice were anesthetized with ketamine/xylazine (120/16 mg/kg body weight), and after disinfection, flanks were incised, the right kidney was clamped for 26 min, and the contralateral kidney was fully removed. Mice received buprenorphine for three more days (0.1 mg/kg) to achieve analgesia. For genetic fate tracing of Gli1
+
cells, we bred bigenic Gli1CreER;tdTomato using Gli1tm3(re/ERT2)Alj/J (Jackson Laboratory stock no. 007913) and Rosa26tdTomato [i.e., B6-Cg-Gt(ROSA)26Sorttm(CAG-tdTomato)Hze/J, Jackson Laboratory stock no. 007909] mice. Six- to 7-week-old male mice (
n
= 7) received 3 × 2 mg tamoxifen in corn oil with 3% ethanol via intraperitoneal injection (every other day) to induce recombination and underwent the unilateral IRI plus contralateral nephrectomy surgery at 21 days after the last tamoxifen dose. Mice were killed 21 weeks after surgery, and the left ventricle was snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and transferred to −80°C. Serum urea was measured by clinical laboratory routine (Vitros 250, Ortho Clinical Diagnostics, Institut für Versuchstierkunde, Aachen). Heart weights were recorded (Sartorius 2007 MP, Germany) and normalized to tibia length, measured by a caliper (Forum, Germany).
Animal experiment protocols were approved by the Landesamt für Natur, Umwelt und Verbraucherschutz Nordrhein Westfalen LANUV-NRW, Germany and by the UK Home Office Regulations. All animal experiments were carried out in accordance with their guidelines.
Human hearts (
n
= 6 to 7) were collected as parts of the Cardiac Aging IN CKD CAIN cohort and by the National Disease Research Interchange (NDRI) and approved by the Partners Institutional Review Board (protocol no. 2017P001244/PHS).
Echocardiography
Echocardiography was performed on a Visualsonics Vevo 770 or 3100 in 2% isoflurane anesthesia. Thoracic fur was removed by depilatory cream, and mice were fixed on a heated table (37°C). A parasternal long-axis view of the heart was used to obtain electrocardiogram-gated kilohertz visualization over one cardiac cycle. Ejection fraction was measured by the Simpson’s method using four biplane views in B mode. Spectral Doppler was carried out in parasternal short-axis view and used to assess mitral valve and blood flow.
Millar
Hemodynamic parameters were measured by Millar catheter (Millar Instruments, USA). Mice were anesthetized with 10 μl/g body weight of ketamine (100 mg/kg) and xylazine (10 mg/kg), and 1 Fr Millar catheter (SPR 1000) was advanced across the right carotid artery through the aortic valve into the left ventricle. After hemodynamic stabilization, signals were continuously recorded and analyzed with iox (Emka Technologies, France). After a constant baseline signal, mice were injected with 5 μl/g body weight of dobutamine (1 mg/ml) to achieve maximal heart function.
Nuclei isolation
All steps were performed at 4°C. The same region from the apex of the snap-frozen left ventricle from each heart was cut and thawed in AW medium (Cellutron Life Technologies, USA). Left ventricular specimens from two mice hearts were pooled to one sample. Pieces were transferred to tris buffer [10 mM tris-HCl, 10 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl
2
, 0.1% NP-40, ribonuclease inhibitor (0.2 U/ml; Protector, Roche, Switzerland)] and 1× protease inhibitor (Roche cOmplete, Roche, Switzerland) in nuclease-free water (Invitrogen by Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). A tissue grinder was used to homogenize the tissues, and the lysate was incubated for 10 min on ice. The lysate was diluted with AW medium and further disrupted by pipetting up and down with a 2-ml glass pipette. The homogenate was filtered with a 70-μm cell strainer and centrifuged at 300
g
for 5 min. The pellet was washed twice with 1% bovine serum albumin (Ultra Pure, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) with protease inhibitor and filtered over a 40-μm cell strainer. The nuclei solution was subjected to single-nuclei sorting on a Sony SH800 cell sorter (Sony Biotechnologies, USA) over a 70-μm nozzle.
Single-nuclei sequencing
Next, nuclei were counted manually in a Neubauer chamber and loaded onto a 10× Chromium B chip and further processed according to the manufacturer’s´ instructions (Chromium Single-Cell Kit V3, 10x Genomics, USA). Briefly, gel beads in emulsion (GEM) were generated and barcoded (Chromium, 10x Genomics, USA). GEMs were cleaned, and complementary DNA (cDNA) was amplified on a thermal cycler (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). The cDNA was cleaned by SPRIselect beads, and a quality check was performed on a tape station. The cDNA library was generated after fragmentation, indexing, and double-sided size selection.
The library quality was determined using D1000 ScreenTape on a 2200 TapeStation system (Agilent Technologies, USA). Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq (Illumina Inc., USA) targeting a read depth as suggested by 10x Genomics 3′ single-cell RNA kits V2/3.
Cell culture
Human AC16 cardiomyocytes (Merck Millipore, USA) were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM)–F12 (D6434 Sigma-Aldrich, Germany) supplemented with 2 mM glutamine (TMS-002-C Millipore, USA), 12.5% fetal bovine serum (ES-009-B Millipore, USA), and 1% penicillin/streptomycin. For treatment, medium was supplemented either with 5 or 10% serum, pooled from healthy donors or pooled from dialysis patients, and incubated for 3 days at 37°C and 5% CO
2
. Cells were further treated with 100 nM Edn1 (Sigma-Aldrich, Germany), 500 nM ruxolitinib (Abcam, Germany) + 5% uremic serum or 50 μM etanercept + uremic serum, or vehicle for 3 days at 37°C and 5% CO
2
. For phosphoproteomics, AC16 cells and immortalized human cardiac PDGFRB cells (
59
) were treated with 5% healthy or 5% uremic serum for 90 min and 3 days. Afterward, PBS washed cells were lysed in 5% SDS, 5 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine, 10 mM chloroacetamide, and 100 mM tris (pH 8.5) at 95°C for 10 min.
HUVECs were isolated from primary tissue as previously described (
60
). Briefly, the umbilical cord vein was rinsed with 10% Hepes buffer (Life Technologies, Germany) using a butterfly syringe to remove the remaining blood. Afterward, the vein was filled with collagenase type I (330 U/ml; Worthington, USA), and the umbilical cord was incubated in 37°C prewarmed PBS (Gibco, Germany). To avoid leakage of collagenase, the umbilical cord was fixed with clamps. After 20 min, the vein was washed with 10 ml of 10% Hepes buffer in DMEM high glucose. Following a 7-min centrifugation step (200 g), the buffer was removed and the cell pellet was resuspended in 10 ml of EBM-2 Bullet Kit Medium (Lonza, Germany). Cells were seeded in a 75-cm
2
tissue culture flask coated with 2% gelatin (Sigma-Aldrich, Germany). After 24 hours, the first adherent island-like clusters with cobble-stone morphology were visible. HUVECs were cultured in a 20% O
2
, 5% CO
2
humidified atmosphere at 37°C. Endothelial cells were isolated from umbilical cords after cesarian sections and after informed consent, according to the standards of the local Ethics Committee (EK116/19).
For tube assay, HUVECs were cultured on Matrigel (Corning, Fisher Scientific, USA) overnight. Cells were treated with either uremic or healthy serum, as well as Edn1 protein (LS-
G26630
/108739, Biozol, Germany) or Edn1 neutralizing antibody (Ab 2786, Abcam, UK) to isotype control. Tubes were imaged on a BZ9001 Biorevo microscope (Keyence, Japan) and analyzed by the angiogenesis analyzer ImageJ plug-in (
61
).
The uremic serum was gathered from hemodialysis patients immediately before dialysis or healthy volunteers after informed consent. The study was approved by the ethical board of the RWTH Aachen University Hospital (Ethical Vote 347/15) and performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Cell lysis, protein extraction, and digestion
Cells were lysed with boiling SDS buffer [5% SDS, 5 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine, 10 mM chloroacetamide, and 100 mM tris (pH 8.5)]. Lysates were heated at 95°C for 10 min while shaking and further sonicated by microtip probe sonication (Vibra-Cell VCX130, Sonics, Newtown, CT) for 2 min with pulses of 1-s on and 1-s off at 70% amplitude. Protein concentration was estimated by bicinchoninic acid (Pierce).
Protein was digested using the protein aggregation capture protocol. One milligram of protein was resuspended with acetonitrile (ACN) to a final 70% concentration. MagReSyn Hydroxyl beads were added in a proportion of 1:2 (protein:beads). Protein aggregation was performed in two steps of 1-min mixing at 1000 rpm, followed by 10-min pause each. Beads were subsequently washed three times with 1 ml of 95% ACN and two times with 1 ml of 70% EtOH. Three hundred microliters of digestion buffer (50 mM ammonium bicarbonate) and proteases was added in the following proportions: trypsin 1:250 (enzyme:protein) and lysC 1:500 (enzyme:protein). Digestion was carried out overnight at 37°C with looping mixing. Protease activity was quenched by acidification with trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) to a final concentration of 1%.
Seven hundred fifty nanograms of digested peptides for single-shot proteome analysis was loaded on C18 Evotips (Evosep) for mass spectrometry (MS) analysis, and the remaining peptide mixture was concentrated on Sep-Pak (C18 Classic Cartridge, Waters, Milford, MA). Peptides were eluted with 150 μl of 40% ACN, followed by 150 μl of 60% ACN. The combined eluate was reduced by SpeedVac (Eppendorf, Germany), and the final peptide concentration was estimated by measuring absorbance at 280 nm on a NanoDrop 2000C spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific).
Phosphoproteomic enrichment
Fifty micrograms of peptides was dried by SpeedVac and resuspended with 200 μl of loading buffer (80% ACN, 5%TFA, and 1 M glycolic acid). Subsequent phospho-enrichment was performed in the King-fisher robot using 20 μl of MagReSyn Ti-IMAC HP beads (20 mg/ml). The unbound peptides were enriched a second time. Enriched phosphopeptides were acidified with 10% TFA until pH < 3, filtered to remove in-suspension particles (1 min, 500 g; MultiScreenHTS HV Filter Plate, 0.45 μm, clear, nonsterile), and loaded on C18 Evotips (Evosep) for MS analysis.
MS analysis
Samples were analyzed on the Evosep One system coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 480. Samples for proteome analysis were separated on an in-house packed 15-cm analytical column (150 μm inner diameter) and packed with 1.9-μm C18 beads, and column temperature was maintained at 60°C using an integrated column oven (PRSO-V1, Sonation GmbH). Samples for phosphoproteomics analysis were analyzed using EV-1112 column (PepSep; 15 cm × 75 μm, beads 1.9 μm) and EV-1087 emitter (fused silica, 20 μm). The column temperature was maintained at 40°C using a butterfly heater (PST-ES-BPH-20, Phoenix S&T) and interfaced online using an EASY-Spray source with the Orbitrap Exploris 480 MS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bremen, Germany) using Xcalibur. Preprogrammed gradients were used as follows: 30 samples per day for proteome and 20 samples per day for phosphoproteome (Whisper method).
The mass spectrometer was operated in a positive ion mode, with spray voltage at 2 kV for proteome and 1.8 kV for phosphoproteome. The heated capillary temperature was set at 275°C and the funnel radio frequency (RF) at 40. Peptide match was set to off, and isotope exclusion was on.
Data-independent acquisition (DIA) mode was used for both proteome and phosphoproteome. For proteome and phosphoproteome, full MS resolution was set to 120,000 at a mass/charge ratio (
m
/
z
) of 200, and full MS automatic gain control (AGC) target was set at 300%, with an injection time of 45 ms, and scan range was set to 350 to 1400
m
/
z
. AGC target value for fragment scan was set at 1000%. Normalized collision energy was set at 27%. For proteome, 49 windows of 13.7 Da were used with an overlap of 1 Da. The MS/MS acquisition was set to 15,000 resolution, and injection time was set to 22 ms. Normalized collision energy was set at 27%. For phosphoproteome, 26 windows of 25.9 Da were used with an overlap of 1 Da. The MS/MS acquisition was set to 30,000 resolution, and injection time was set to 54 ms.
MS raw data processing
DIA data were analyzed with Spectronaut v15.6.211220.50606 in directDIA mode with standard settings. The Human UniProt fasta file (downloaded in October 2020; 20,600 entries) was supplemented with a contaminant fasta file containing 246 entries.
Staining of tissue and cells
Cardiomyocytes were stained with tetramethylrhodamine (TMRM) (T668, Sigma-Aldrich, Germany) at 100 nM concentration and incubated for 30 min at 37°C. Images were taken on a Nikon A1 laser confocal microscope (Nikon, Tokio, Japan).
To analyze the size of cardiomyocytes and the capillary density, tissue sections were rehydrated and heat-induced antigen retrieval was performed in citrate buffer. Slides were incubated with fluorescein-coupled WGA (1:100; FL-1021, Vector Laboratories) and CD31 (1:50; AF3628, R&D Systems) and further counterstained with DAPI. Slides were digitalized using Aperio Versa200 whole-slide scanner (Leica Biosystems, Germany). For each mouse, three areas from the inner part of the left ventricle were analyzed using ImageJ (National Institutes of Health). 3

In situ hybridizations were performed with the RNAscope multiplex fluorescent reagent kit V2 assay (ACD, Biotechne, USA) on heart cryosections, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Probes were designed against
Pecam1
and
Edn1
. Sections were counterstained with DAPI, embedded in Immumount, and imaged on a Nikon A1 laser confocal microscope (Nikon, Tokio, Japan).
Single-cell RNA analysis
We preprocessed scRNA-seq sequencing data for each library with cellranger pipeline (v3.1.0) using the default parameters. Next, we used Seurat [v3.2.0; (
62

Next, we filtered cells by only retaining cells with nFeatureRNAfloor of >400 and nCountRNAceilling of <40,000. We used the function FindIntegrationAchors and IntegrateData to integrate samples followed by calling the function FindNeighbors and FindClusters (resolution = 0.5) to find communities on principal components analysis (PCA) embedding space (pcs = 30).
Differentially expressed genes enrichment analysis
We retrieved highly expressed differential marker genes using FindAllMarkers and annotated clusters with curated markers. Next, we applied clusterProfiler [v3.18.0; (
63

https://maayanlab.cloud/Harmonizome/gene_set/Hypertrophy/CTD+Gene-Disease+Associations
, standardizedValue>2)] and (ii) (Capillary changes,
https://maayanlab.cloud/Harmonizome/gene_set/angiogenesis/GeneRIF+Biological+Term+Annotations
). The ECM gene set used in this study was obtained from Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA). Specifically, the ECM gene set corresponds to the NABA_CORE_MATRISOME item included in MSigDB. To plot ridges of these gene sets, we calculated the gene module score(
x
axis) by summing the gene expressions and obtaining the log-normalized value of the score.
Trajectory inference
To do trajectory analysis for a specific cell type population, we first selected a subpopulation of this cell type. Next, we embedded the PCA to a diffusion map using destiny [v3.4.0; (
64
,
66
)], followed by clustering on the embedding space. We performed the similar strategy of ArchR [v1.0.1; (
67
)] to do the trajectory analysis. We first defined a backbone by selecting cluster IDs. Next, we calculated mean coordinates for each cluster and Euclidean distance of each cell from cluster i to mean coordinate of cluster i + 1. Next, we fitted a trajectory using smooth spline function and scaled the pseudotime to 100. To construct genes along the trajectory matrix, we first split cells to 100 groups by their pseudotime ranges. We next summed up each group of cells to get a matrix, followed by log-normalizing on the matrix. The GO term matrix was constructed on the basis of the genes along the trajectory matrix. We first split the pseudotime into five groups, and we decided the group of each gene by its highest mean expression of the group. With the five gene sets, we then ran GO enrichment to get the GO terms along the trajectory.

t
test with independent variance was applied to check for differences between two groups for parametric data. Three groups were compared by ordinary one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with multiple comparisons as a follow-up test. The significance level was set to
P
< 0.05. The software GraphPad Prism 9 and IBM statistics SPSS 26 were used. Student’s
t
